title: Queue throttle + netns leak diary
content:
Summary:

On 2025-01-17 we observed a progressive degradation in pod scheduling throughput in the eu-west region correlated with node-level network namespace count growth on a subset of GPU-backed worker nodes. The symptom at the application level was long scheduling queue latency (p95 > 8s) and a spike in Pending pods. In parallel some GPU pods reported degraded attach/driver errors. The incident appears to be a mix of a kernel netns leak (or stale veth namespaces from rapid pod churn) and scheduler backpressure that amplified the user-visible impact.

Why this doc exists:
- Capture rough timeline from oncall shift (notes to hand over)
- Record transient mitigation steps that helped restore capacity
- Draft a detection + automated mitigation runbook for next time
- Surface follow-ups (kernel, kube-proxy, CNI, GC tuning)

Immediate timeline (notes from pager):
- 02:12 UTC: Alert SRE: scheduler-p95 > 8s (threshold 2s) and Pending pods increased > 120 across eu-west cluster.
- 02:15 UTC: Paging channel: multiple pods stuck in "ContainerCreating" with messages mentioning network plugins and attach errors for GPU devices.
- 02:18 UTC: Ran kubectl get nodes -o wide; 18 of 120 nodes reported NotReady transiently, most GPU-annotated nodes had elevated load.
- 02:22 UTC: Observed unusual growth in /proc/net/netns entries on affected nodes (manually inspected); netns count ~1200 vs baseline ~80.
- 02:35 UTC: Evicted a problem node and restarted kubelet; some pod scheduling cleared locally.
- 03:05 UTC: Applied short-term mitigation: cordon slow nodes + scaled up a pre-warmed pool (non-GPU) to absorb queued workloads. Scheduling p95 improved to ~2.3s by 03:20 UTC.

Key signals and telemetry observed:
- kube-scheduler: scheduling attempts per second dropped by ~40% during the window; scheduling retries rose.
- kubelet logs: repeated CNI plugin timeouts, "failed to setup network for pod" messages, and occasional "couldn't find network namespace" traces.
- Node kernel: /proc/net/netns count increasing linearly with churn. lsof/ss showing large numbers of sockets tied to stale netns.
- Node memory: minor growth in kernel slab caches related to netfilter tables, but not full OOM.
- conntrack: per-node conntrack entries surged on affected nodes causing higher system CPU on netfilter path.
- GPU attach logs: NVidia container runtime occasionally failed to find vGPU device mapping while netns cleanup was ongoing.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) CNI plugin (weave/plugX) failing to cleanup netns/veth on rapid pod churn leading to netns leak -> kernel resources consumed -> CNI RPC timeouts -> kubelet reports network failures -> scheduler defers pod placement causing queueing.
2) kube-proxy or iptables rules accumulating per-netns state causing conntrack growth and CPU interference, slowing kubelet and kube-scheduler heartbeats.
3) Underlying kernel version + driver bug causing netns objects to linger after container shim exits (needs kernel debug).
4) A secondary effect: GPU attach path's reliance on timely network namespace teardown caused device binding race and additional pod failures.

Quick on-call mitigations attempted and their effects:
- Cordoning nodes with netns > 500 and cordon + drain did not always succeed (drain hung due to ContainerCreating states) but cordon prevented further scheduling to affected hosts. Immediate reduction in queue growth.
- Restarted kubelet on 3 worst nodes (rolling) — this freed up netns and allowed normal pod setup to proceed on those nodes. Helps but disruptive (restarts cause rescheduling).
- Temporarily scaled non-GPU prewarm pool (fast nodes) to reduce pressure on GPU queue — reduced Pending count but required config approvals from cluster auto-scaler team.
- Manual cleanup attempts (ip netns delete XXX) on nodes removed many stale netns but was not safe to run across all nodes.
- Applied a short-lived admission-rate limiter on API server (via temporary rate-limiting feature gating) to reduce pod create storm; reduced churn and slowed netns growth.

Commands used during triage (notes):
- Check netns count: ls -1 /proc/*/ns/net | wc -l  (gives rough live count)
- Find netns usage: sudo find /var/run/netns -type s -maxdepth 1 -ls; ip netns list
- Identify process holding netns: for pid in $(ls /proc | egrep '^[0-9]+$'); do readlink /proc/$pid/ns/net | sed -n 's/.*net:\[\(//p'; done  (manual mapping)
- conntrack stats: sudo conntrack -S; watch -n1 "cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count"
- kernel slab debug: sudo slabtop -s c | head -n 30
- kube-scheduler metrics: curl localhost:10259/metrics | grep scheduling_duration_seconds

Immediate follow-ups (actionable):
- SRE: Add an automated netns-growth alert (threshold: netns_count > 300 and sustained > 5m) per node.
- SRE/Platform: Add node-level conntrack saturation alert (nf_conntrack_count > 500k) tied to scheduling latency events.
- Infra: Run kernel + CNI version matrix validation on a smaller repro cluster; attempt to reproduce with pod churn tool (see linked artifact SRE-4827).
- Eng (CNI owners): Add better defensive cleanup in CNI plugin for veth/netns teardown; add metrics for cleanup failures.
- Platform: Create a safe, automated netns pruning job that targets orphaned netns older than X minutes and logs actions (must be opt-in and guarded).
- Investigate whether kubelet's max-pods and pod churn interacts with CNI GC; consider conservative defaults for GPU pools.

Draft runbook (first-pass):
Title: Detect and mitigate excessive network namespaces causing scheduler queue throttling
Scope: Nodes exhibiting unexplained increases in netns count, pod create failures referencing CNI or network setup timeouts, and concurrent increase in scheduling latency.
Preconditions: cluster-admin privileges, runbook executes only for non-control-plane worker nodes.
Detection:
- Run node check: netns_count=$(ls -1 /proc/*/ns/net | wc -l); report if > 300 for > 5m.
- Cross-check kubelet log for "failed to setup network for pod" pattern.
Mitigation steps (ordered, safe-first):
1) Cordon affected node: kubectl cordon <node>; note node annotation with "sre.netns.cordoned=true"
2) Try graceful drain with timeout and force only if safe: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=5m
   - If drain hangs due to ContainerCreating: capture pod list and skip problematic pods for manual handling.
3) Attempt non-disruptive netns cleanup: sudo ip -all netns | grep orphan || (sudo find /proc/*/ns/net -lname "*" -printf...)  (manual pattern — requires helper script)
4) If cleanup not feasible, perform kubelet restart: sudo systemctl restart kubelet (note: this will evict pods)
5) If restart does not reduce netns count or node unhealthy: replace node via autoscaler (terminate instance)
6) After recovery: uncordon: kubectl uncordon <node> and annotate runbook steps in ticket.
Postmortem checklist items:
- Capture full /proc/*/ns/net snapshot before any destructive steps (for kernel devs)
- Kernel coredump (if reproducible) and netns object tracking logs
- CNI plugin debug logs for times of teardown failures and xid/txn ids
- kubelet/gc configuration review (eviction thresholds, pod-max, dead container GC interval)

Open questions / research items:
- Is this a known regression in kernel X.Y.Z vs X.Y.Z-1? Need to reproduce and check LKML/bugtracker.
- Are there CNI call patterns where veth deletion races with containerd/CRI leaving dangling netns?
- Should we add a node-level periodic netns GC agent or expand containerd's cleanup responsibilities?
- How to safely run ip netns cleanup at scale without corrupting live namespaces? Need a careful heuristic (older-than + unreferenced by any PID).

Notes to next on-call (handoff):
- Key metric to watch: scheduler_p95 (kube-scheduler) + netns_count (per-node) + nf_conntrack_count
- If you see another spike: cordon early, scale prewarm pool, avoid mass kubelet restarts unless node-level cleanup fails.
- Use SRE-4821 to track mitigation progress and SRE-4827 for reproduction harness.

Appendix: useful helper scripts (rough)
- netns-inspect.sh (pseudo):
  #!/bin/bash
  for ns in $(ls -1 /proc/*/ns/net 2>/dev/null); do
    pid=$(echo $ns | cut -d'/' -f3)
    echo "pid:$pid -> $(readlink $ns) -> $(ps -p $pid -o cmd= 2>/dev/null)"
  done

- safe-prune-netns.sh (very conservative draft):
  # collect netns not referenced by any running pid and older than 30m, log to /var/log/netns-prune.log, do NOT delete automatically until reviewed.

References & links:
- Jira SRE-4821 (Incident ticket)
- Jira SRE-4827 (Repro harness + load generator)
- Infra PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/912 (prewarm pool autoscale change)

Hand-off state: in_review (need kernel/CNI owners to validate the hypothesis and sign off on netns GC implementation plan).

Notes to self: keep wording light in public postmortem; this doc is intentionally technical and messy — will be distilled for the postmortem writeup.
